French West Africa was a federation of eight French colonies in West Africa, from 1895 to 1958, governed from Saint-Louis and, after 1902, Dakar. The map shows it from 1914 to 1938. It was about eight times the size of France.

Its colonies became today's:

  • Senegal, Mauritania, Mali (then French Sudan), Guinea, Ivory Coast, Burkina Faso (then Upper Volta), Benin (then Dahomey) and Niger.

A governor-general in Dakar ran it, and most Africans were subjects, not citizens. Only people born in Senegal's four old towns had French citizenship; in 1914 they elected Blaise Diagne, the first Black African in the French parliament.

The federation sent nearly 200,000 African soldiers, the Tirailleurs Sénégalais, to fight for France in the First World War. Groundnuts from Senegal, cotton and rice from the Office du Niger, and cocoa and coffee from Ivory Coast were its main exports.

After 1945 African parties grew, led by figures such as Félix Houphouët-Boigny and Léopold Sédar Senghor. The federation was broken up in 1958, and its members became independent states in 1958 and 1960. The CFA franc, its shared currency, still links most of them to France.
sum: French West Africa was a federation of eight French colonies in West Africa, from 1895 to 1958, governed from Saint-Louis and, after 1902, Dakar. The map shows it from 1914 to 1938. It was about eight times the size of France.
